Week 1 · Day 1: The research-to-production workflow

Learning objective: Use the 3rd edition of Stefan Jansen’s Machine Learning for Trading to move from a specific economic or engineering question to testable evidence. Today is a 150-minute (2 h 30 min) session including careful reading, inspected runnable examples, independent implementation and a short scientific write-up. The goal is defensible quant research, not memorizing formulas or producing an attractive equity curve.

Book reading and official chapter code

  • Chapter 1: The Process Is Your Edge (starts on printed p. 1) — official companion chapter guide and notebooks. Read the sections relevant to today’s four subtopics, then select one representative notebook; completing every chapter notebook in one session is not required.

Page references are printed chapter-start anchors from the 2026 table of contents, not claims about exact subtopic or eBook/PDF page locations. Your copy may use different viewer pagination.

Subtopics explained

1. The seven research stages

Separate problem definition, acquisition, feature generation, learning, evaluation, portfolio translation, and deployment. Give each stage an input artifact and a testable output rather than treating a high backtest Sharpe as the endpoint.

Study reference: Chapter 1: The Process Is Your Edge (starts on printed p. 1); chapter notebook guide; supplementary source: github.

2. Hypothesis before model

An economic mechanism should explain why a signal might persist after costs. State the forecast horizon, eligible instruments, how frequently positions can change, and what alternative explanations could invalidate the claim.

Study reference: Chapter 1: The Process Is Your Edge (starts on printed p. 1); chapter notebook guide; supplementary source: case etf.

3. Evidence boundary

Distinguish exploratory development data from validation and an untouched final holdout. Repeatedly tuning on test results converts the test into a training set, even if no target column appears in the features.

Study reference: Chapter 1: The Process Is Your Edge (starts on printed p. 1); chapter notebook guide; supplementary source: github.

4. Research traceability

Record data versions, timestamps, source licenses, parameters, seeds, notebooks and decisions. A reproducible rejection of a bad strategy is a successful research result, not wasted work.

Study reference: Chapter 1: The Process Is Your Edge (starts on printed p. 1); chapter notebook guide; supplementary source: case etf.

150-minute study plan

  1. 0–35 min: Read the assigned chapter sections; sketch four core ideas and write one hypothesis or assumption.
  2. 35–70 min: Inspect the corresponding official chapter README and one notebook; note its data contracts, tests and inputs.
  3. 70–130 min: Implement the practical assignment, save executable code, tests and figures.
  4. 130–150 min: Write a 150–250 word experiment memo, inspect leakage/cost risks, and record the next question.

Practical assignment (150-minute lesson)

Write a one-page research charter for a liquid ETF rotation idea; add a falsifiable null hypothesis, data cutoff, benchmark, and no-trade criteria.

Scientific checks and research journal

  • Time integrity: Identify the observation/event timestamp, when it was publicly available, and when it became an eligible feature. Test at least one off-by-one or future-data failure case.
  • Reproducibility: Save the source data reference, run configuration, package versions, random seed where used, and at least one numerical result or diagnostic figure.
  • Evidence over optimism: State a baseline and a falsification criterion; distinguish exploratory findings from the independent test set. When evaluating trading economics, report costs, turnover and implementation limitations.

Definition of done

Charter explicitly defines what would falsify the idea and which data are forbidden after a prediction timestamp.

Week 1 deliverable connection: Versioned ETF research charter, point-in-time OHLCV panel, data dictionary and automated quality report. Keep your work in a dated notebook or reusable module and include what did not work. The main reference is the purchased book; official code and freely available docs are supporting materials.

1. Asset-class differences

Equities, ETFs, FX, futures, options and crypto differ in trading hours, roll mechanics, contract size, financing and data access. Choose ETFs for the baseline to limit complexity; retain futures as an optional extension.

Define open, high, low, close, volume and adjustment factors, including dividends and splits. Check that signals use only values available at the decision time, rather than revised adjusted histories presented as if known then.

4. Data license and lineage

Log public-vendor provenance, fetch date, coverage and restrictions. Prefer a modest lawful dataset over a huge black-box data dump that cannot be reproduced or shared.

Historical index membership and current ticker lists omit failures and inflate retrospective returns. Explain how a point-in-time universe should include securities that subsequently disappear.

Study reference: Chapter 2: The Financial Data Universe (starts on printed p. 21); chapter notebook guide; supplementary source: polars.

2. Event time versus availability time

A record can describe yesterday yet arrive tomorrow. Maintain event_time, ingestion_time and available_at columns; join every explanatory observation using when it became usable.

Study reference: Chapter 2: The Financial Data Universe (starts on printed p. 21); chapter notebook guide; supplementary source: bias.

3. Corporate actions and stale marks

Adjusted prices, halted instruments and vendor forward fills can create synthetic opportunities. Detect stale prices, zero-volume bars and suspicious return jumps before building features.

4. Missingness mechanisms

Differentiate missing-at-random gaps, planned market closures and vendor outages. Do not fill missing values with a future observation or silently delete difficult trading days.

1. Orders versus trades

A limit order adds displayed liquidity; a trade consumes it; a cancel removes it. Exchange feed messages are not identical to executed trades, so record each event type separately.

Study reference: Chapter 3: Market Microstructure (starts on printed p. 47); chapter notebook guide; supplementary source: case futures.

2. Price-time priority

In a basic continuous limit book, better price precedes worse price and earlier resting orders lead within a level. The real matching rules vary by venue; do not generalize one simulator to every market.

Study reference: Chapter 3: Market Microstructure (starts on printed p. 47); chapter notebook guide; supplementary source: case futures.

3. Top-of-book state

Calculate best bid, best ask, spread, midpoint and depth after every event. Verify invariants and discuss locked, crossed or stale books as possible quality problems.

Study reference: Chapter 3: Market Microstructure (starts on printed p. 47); chapter notebook guide; supplementary source: case futures.

4. Exchange event sequencing

Preserve sequence numbers and replay gaps rather than manufacturing state transitions. Relate book reconstruction to your FIX/feed engineering experience without assuming a drop-copy trade stream reconstructs full order-book state.
